summary: Ages 7-8: read and write numbers to 1000 across three registers — numerals (342), number names ('three hundred and forty-two') and expanded form (300 + 40 + 2) — and translate fluently in both directions. The hardest cases are the spoken→written mapping and internal/placeholder zeros (306, 340, 305). Expanded form acts as an explicit bridge from number names to place value. Core activities give learners genuine two-way production (encode and decode) anchored to a base-ten build; a static reference wall and light oral reading are preserved as scaffolds with stated limits.
misconceptions: Writing what you hear literally: 'three hundred and six' → 3006 or 30006.
Dropping or misplacing internal zeros (340 written as 34; 306 as 36).
Mis-ordering words vs digits, or omitting the hundreds word.
Confusing teen and -ty words within the tens part (forty vs fourteen).
Treating expanded form as separate numbers (300, 40, 2) rather than a partition of one number.

activities.title: Three-pane number translator (build, type, name)
steps: Work with three linked views of one number side by side: a numeral display, a word-tile builder, and an expanded-form strip, with a base-ten build (flats/rods/cubes) shown beneath.

Change any one view and watch the others and the blocks rebuild: assemble the word-tiles 'three hundred and forty-two' and confirm 342 appears alongside 300 + 40 + 2 and three flats, four rods, two cubes.
Translate deliberately in BOTH directions: read a shown numeral and build its words; and start from spoken/word form and write the numeral.
Sequence difficulty: start with no-zero numbers (342), then one internal zero (306), then a trailing zero (340).
activities.insight: Numeral, words and expanded form are three views of ONE number; expanded form reveals each digit's place value, and the empty column shows why a placeholder zero must be written (306, not 36 or 3006).

activities.title: Two-way translation practice (write it, name it, expand it)
steps: Write a spoken or word-form number as a numeral (e.g. write 'six hundred and forty' as 640).
Write a given numeral in words (e.g. write 306 as 'three hundred and six').
Complete expanded form from a numeral (e.g. 485 = 400 + __ + 5) and the reverse.
Match numeral ↔ words ↔ expanded form for a set of numbers, deliberately including internal-zero and trailing-zero cases (305, 340).
Decide the correct written form among plausible errors for internal-zero numbers.
activities.insight: Both encode (spoken/words → numeral) and decode (numeral → words) directions become reliable, especially for the zero traps and the tens digit's place value.

activities.title: Reference wall: one number in three registers
steps: Study a fixed anchor card showing 342 as numeral, words and expanded form at once, with a base-ten build.
Tap the words to highlight the matching digits and expanded parts (where an interactive display is available).
Open a 306 'card flap' that explains why the 0 is written in the tens place.
activities.insight: Seeing all three registers of the same number aligned, with the placeholder zero explained, gives a stable mental model to refer back to.

activities.title: Read-it-back oral warm-up
steps: Listen to a spoken three-digit number and read a number back aloud.
Say aloud the number shown on a card, attending to the connective 'and' and the hundreds word.
activities.insight: Hearing and saying numbers aloud rehearses the spoken register and the 'and' connective, supporting the spoken→written mapping.

checkQuestion: Watch the child read and write. 'Read 342 aloud. Now write “three hundred and forty-two” as a numeral. Write 637 in expanded form. Now write 305 in words, and in expanded form.' The 305 item is the key — watch the zero.
checkAnswer: Reads 342 correctly; writes 342; 637 = 600 + 30 + 7; 305 = 'three hundred and five' and 300 + 5 (with 0 tens).
